extracted.intended_audience: serious narrative prose writers and workshop participants (not beginners)
extracted.subtask_description: A handbook/workbook for experienced writers focused on the fundamentals of narrative prose (sound, punctuation, sentence rhythm, voice, point of view, etc.), with exercises and workshop procedures to practice and critique those elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound of the language / Does it sound right?
rubrics_metrics.description: THE SOUND OF THE LANGUAGE IS WHERE it all begins. The test of a sentence is, Does it sound right?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train your mind’s ear; read prose aloud; listen for lively, well-paced, flowing, strong, beautiful rhythms. Sound and rhythm affect both meaning and beauty. Use examples and perform them aloud to feel cadence. The sound of sentences embodies emotion and moves the story forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence duty: lead to the next sentence (forward movement, pace, rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence—to keep the story going. Forward movement, pace, and rhythm are primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control rhythm so sentences propel the narrative. Avoid dull, choppy, droning, jerky, or feeble sounds. Arrange sentence rhythms to create pace and forward drive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative must move / story is change
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative is an account of an act or action; it has to move—end up in a different place from where it started. That’s what narrative does. It goes. It moves. Story is change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing exercises or scenes, make them dynamic rather than static. Even quiet scenes must embody change—movement of action, emotion, or situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sound devices in prose (but not poetry metre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use onomatopoeia, alliteration, repetition, rhythmic effects, made-up words or names, dialect—any kind of sound effect you like—but NOT rhyme or meter. This is prose, not poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play with sound effects to create gorgeous prose intended to be read aloud. Use dialect or invented words if appropriate. Avoid regular rhyme and meter when writing prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud / perform to test rhythm and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the piece aloud to yourself or perform it; speaking and hearing it will show awkward bits and faults in rhythm and can help make dialogue natural and lively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud is a key revision tool. In group settings perform pieces and accept applause for performance-oriented pieces; less critiquing may be appropriate for such pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation tells the reader how to hear your writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation tells the reader how to hear your writing. Periods and commas and semicolons make clear the grammar and the emotions by showing what it sounds like—where the breaks come, where to pause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use punctuation intentionally to shape rhythm and meaning. Recommended mapping: period = stop (for a moment), semicolon = pause, comma = brief pause or expect change, dash = pause that sets a phrase apart. Wrong choices can alter or lose meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know grammar vocabulary and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should know grammar terms (subject, predicate, object, adjective, adverb, tenses) because they are the names of the writer’s tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get familiar with grammatical terms so you can diagnose and talk about sentence problems. Consult a grammar manual when in doubt (Chicago Manual of Style, Elements of Style, The Well-Tempered Sentence) but adapt rules to narrative needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness for clarity; improper usage cripples meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorrect usage, unless part of a conscious, consistent dialect or personal voice, is disastrous. Incoherent syntax, mistaken words, misplaced punctuation all cripple meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow shared rules of grammar and usage to make writing clear to readers who lack your vocal cues. Treat correctness as a social agreement for communication, not a moral absolute. Revise to eliminate unintentional errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules may be broken only intentionally and knowingly
rubrics_metrics.description: To break a rule you have to know the rule. A blunder is not a revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you violate grammar, punctuation, or usage, do so deliberately and consistently as part of voice or dialect; accidental violations damage credibility and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t rely blindly on grammar/autocorrect programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Disable grammar/auto-correct programs; they’re on a pitifully low level of competence and will chop your sentences short and stupidify your writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your own judgment and knowledge of grammar rather than defaulting to software corrections. Be responsible for punctuation and syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance before revision / don’t trust immediate self-judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: When you’re satisfied with an exercise, put it away and forbid yourself to look at it again for a while (a day or two at least). We can’t trust our judgment on fresh work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a cooling-off period, reread with revision in mind, read aloud, and look specifically for what’s wordy, ugly, unclear, unnecessary, preachy, careless—what breaks the pace or doesn’t work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exercises methodically to build skill until unconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercises are consciousness-raisers intended to clarify and intensify awareness of elements of prose; practice them until they become skills you do without thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through exercises in order if alone; repeat exercises as warm-ups; practice regularly so craft enables art and becomes automatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity for workshop reading and time-limited writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise pieces don’t have to be highly finished; most will be very short—a paragraph, a page or so. If reading aloud in a group brevity is a necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short set lengths as a discipline. In workshops, set half-hour limits for composing during meetings to simulate pressure; the Lone Navigator can do the same alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop procedure: silence, timed writing, reading aloud, guided critique
rubrics_metrics.description: In group workshops: discuss the exercise, write in silence for a set time (half an hour absolute limit), then each person reads their piece aloud hot off the paper; follow the peer-group procedure in the appendix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure elicits strong writing under pressure and trains writers to produce and receive critique. For performance pieces minimal critiquing is appropriate; otherwise use suggested critique guidelines (see appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as deliberate training (not plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students of composition and painting deliberately imitate great works as training. Imitation is useful; plagiarism is despicable. Label imitations 'in the style of' a published author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate seriously and not as parody; intention matters. Use imitation to learn technique, then discard or transform it—do not pass it off as original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose examples widely and read the classics for craft
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer who wants to write good stuff needs to read great stuff. Reading only fashionable contemporaries limits what you think can be done with English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study varied examples aloud and discuss what writers are doing and why. Bring other examples to a group and analyze approaches to technical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose exercises as narrative (not explanatory): show action/change
rubrics_metrics.description: For exercises it doesn’t matter if you write fiction or nonfiction—narrative is narrative. Try to make each exercise the account of an act or action; it must move and end somewhere different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid static description; even a supermarket aisle or thoughts in a head should move the reader from one state to another. Focus on action and change rather than exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of names and place-names for their sonic and evocative value
rubrics_metrics.description: Names are interesting sounds; the sound of character and place names can be intensely expressive and meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the echo-allusions and aural qualities of names when naming characters and places; choose names that reinforce tone or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for internet/written-speech pitfalls—reread and aim for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanical ease and immediacy of electronic communication are deceptive. People write hurriedly, don’t reread, get misread, and use emoticons as substitutes for clear communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reread and proof electronic writing carefully. Don’t confuse self-expression with communication; write so readers (who can’t hear your voice) can understand complex thought or emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: When critiquing, look for: wordy, ugly, unclear, unnecessary, preachy, careless
rubrics_metrics.description: In revision look for what’s wordy, ugly, unclear, unnecessary, preachy, careless—what breaks the pace, what doesn’t work. Also identify what does work and try to enhance it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist during revision and group critique. Read aloud to help surface awkward rhythms and unnatural dialogue; praise effective parts and aim to bring them out more strongly.
